edge_cases: Missing required form fields results in an error response from Flask.
Adding a book with a duplicate title triggers a redirect back to the add page.
Login with incorrect username or password returns "Invalid credentials".
Updating or deleting a non‑existent title still returns a success message (no existence check).
Searching with an empty term returns all books (the LIKE pattern matches everything).
SQL injection is possible via unsanitized input, but externally it appears as normal success or failure responses.
contract.intent: Expose a web API for basic library management: adding, viewing, searching, updating, and deleting books, plus member login.
invariants: A database connection is always closed before the HTTP response is sent.
All endpoints use the same MySQL credentials and database (LIBRARYDB).
The add_book endpoint treats the Title field as a unique key.
Responses are either plain‑text strings or HTTP redirects; no JSON is produced.
Only the specified HTTP methods (POST for mutations, GET for reads) are accepted.
Form fields must be present; otherwise Flask raises a 400/KeyError before custom logic runs.
io_behavior: POST /add_book with form fields title and author redirects to ./add_book if the title already exists, otherwise redirects to ./view_books.
POST /login_member with form fields username and password returns plain text "Login successful" or "Invalid credentials".
POST /update_book_author with form fields title and new_author returns plain text "Author updated successfully".
POST /delete_book with form field title returns plain text "Book deleted successfully".
GET /search_books?term=... returns a string representation of a list of books whose title or author contains the term.
GET /view_books returns a string representation of a list of all books in the database.
side_effects: Inserts a new row into the Books table when a unique title is added.
Updates the Author column of a Books row matching the given title.
Deletes a Books row matching the given title.
Reads from the Members table to verify login credentials.
Each request opens a MySQL connection and closes it before responding.
Redirect responses cause the client to issue a follow‑up request to the indicated path.

rationale: Endpoints generally follow the contract, but GET routes return JSON instead of plain‑text lists, login adds a 401 status, and SQL injection is mitigated, violating specified edge cases and response invariants.
